title: The reports, reviewed

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pillars, and your line: from the inside. Each pillar with a body and a heart. Which one did you try with its inside in mind? Day one thousand four hundred thirteen.

A message lands in a family group chat late at night. It begins, the Prophet said, and then a beautiful sentence, and then a row of heart emojis. Somebody's aunt has already forwarded it to her other groups. Nobody asks where it came from. This year spent a long stretch on exactly that question. Before a sentence could be called a hadith, scholars wanted to know who said it, who heard it, who passed it on, and whether every one of those people could be trusted. Today, the reports again: how a hadith reaches you.
screen: `THE PROPHET SAID… FORWARDED.` → `WHERE DID IT COME FROM?` → `HOW A HADITH REACHES YOU.`

segments.voice: First, the two halves. A hadith is a report of what the Prophet, peace be upon him, said, did, or approved. Every hadith has a chain, the isnad, and a text, the matn. The chain is the list of people: I heard it from this one, who heard it from that one, all the way back. Second, why the chain mattered so much. In the introduction to Sahih Muslim, a saying is recorded from the early scholar Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak, in paraphrase: the chain is part of the religion, and without it anyone could say whatever they liked. That is the forwarded message problem, named long before phones. Third, how the chain was tested. Scholars wrote about the narrators themselves, the science the year called rijal: was this man truthful, was his memory sharp, did he really meet the one he quoted? And they tested the text too, asking whether it fit the Qur'an and the known sunnah. Then they graded: sahih, sound; hasan, good; da'if, weak; and some reports exposed as fabricated. Fourth, the people who carried it. Students traveled to hear a report from its source. They memorized chains by heart. Women carried it as well, from Aisha onward, and the year met Karimah al-Marwaziyyah, who taught Bukhari's Sahih. The same introduction to Sahih Muslim carries a warning, in paraphrase: it is enough of a lie for a person to pass on everything they hear. That sentence could sit above every share button. The chain holds because people checked it, link by link.
screen: `A CHAIN AND A TEXT.` · `WITHOUT THE CHAIN, ANYONE SAYS ANYTHING.` · `TESTED, THEN GRADED.` · `CARRIED BY MEMORY AND TRAVEL.`

segments.voice: The practice: share a sound hadith. Settle into the sit, and breathe. Bring to mind one hadith you have met this year whose source you actually know: actions are by intentions, from Bukhari, or none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself, also Bukhari. Hold its words for a few breaths. Then think of one person who might be glad to hear it. Later today, if you like, send it to them, with its source attached, the way the scholars would have wanted. The bell holds the time.
The reports. Hadith: what the Prophet said, did, or approved, each carried by a chain of named people and tested before it was trusted. Today's word.

Your line: the chain holds. Today, before you forward anything, a quote, a news story, a hadith, ask one question first: who said it, and how do I know? Tomorrow, the schools, reviewed. Day one thousand four hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Muslims read hadith in collections such as Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, and Shia Muslims in their own collections such as al-Kafi; scholars grade each report by its chain and its text, and teachers often give the source and grade when they quote one.

fork.setup: a beautiful saying lands in your group chat: "the Prophet said…" no source. what would the hadith scholars do?
options: forward it fast; it sounds good.
ask who narrated it and whether the chain and text hold up.
fork.reveal: they asked for the chain. a saying in Sahih Muslim's introduction puts it this way: without the chain, anyone could say whatever they liked.

original.note: Arabic: the chain of narrators that carries a report back to its source.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hadith is a nice saying of the Prophet.
what it means: a report with a chain of named people and a text, tested and graded before it is trusted.
what a scholar hears: isnad and matn, rijal, the grades sahih, hasan and da'if, and Ibn al-Mubarak's line that the chain is part of the religion.
